blocks.text: Elements may also be categorised by families, sets of elements sharing common properties. The famous families are the alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr), alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Ba, Ra), transition metals (Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn), chalcogens (O, S, Se, Te, Po), halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At, Ts) and noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, Og).

items: Alkali metals: the elements of group 1, so called because they produce alkalis when they react with water; sodium and potassium are notable examples. They have one valence electron, low densities, relatively low melting points and low ionization energies, and are the most reactive metals.

Alkaline earth metals: the group 2 metals, found primarily in the earth and forming alkalis, hence the name; calcium and magnesium are examples. They have two valence electrons, so they are divalent; they are metallic solids, harder and denser than the alkali metals, easily oxidised, with high thermal and electrical conductivities.

Transition elements: the largest family, in the middle of the table. They include the four series of d block elements and the lanthanides and actinides (f block) in the two rows below. They show high thermal and electrical conductivities, high melting points, high density and variable oxidation states, and mostly form coloured compounds.

Chalcogens: the group 16 elements, named because most ores of copper (Greek chalkos) are oxides or sulfides. Oxygen and sulfur are non-metals, Se, Te and Po are metalloids, and livermorium is a metal.

Halogens: the non-metals of group 17. The name means salt-former, because they react readily with the alkali and alkaline earth metals to form stable halide salts; fluorine, chlorine and bromine are examples. They are highly reactive, with high electron affinities, and easily accept one electron to complete their outermost shell.

Noble gases: the unreactive elements of group 18 at the extreme right of the table; helium and argon are examples. With their stable, complete outermost shells they are almost entirely unreactive under normal conditions, rarely form compounds, and are monoatomic.

blocks.title: Keep in mind
blocks.text: Although the noble gases are unreactive, they do have some compounds. An example is a compound of xenon, xenon hexafluoroplatinate (XePtF6); because of such compounds the name inert gases was changed to noble gases.

blocks.prompt: Why are the elements of groups 1 and 2 called s block elements, and which family is named after copper ores?
blocks.explanation: Groups 1 and 2 have their valence electrons in an s subshell, one for group 1 and two for group 2, so they are the s block. The chalcogens, group 16, take their name from the Greek chalkos because most copper ores are oxides or sulfides of these elements.

items: Six families: alkali metals (group 1, one valence electron, most reactive metals), alkaline earth metals (group 2, divalent, harder and denser), transition metals (d and f blocks, variable oxidation states, coloured compounds), chalcogens (group 16, copper-ore formers), halogens (group 17, salt formers, high electron affinity) and noble gases (group 18, full shells, monoatomic; a few xenon compounds exist).
